newsitem.title: USA: Judge says W.Va. trust fund is unconstitutional.
newsitem.headline: Judge says W.Va. trust fund is unconstitutional.

text.p: The West Virginia Trust Fund established by legislators to invest state money in the stock market is unconstitutional, a judge ruled Tuesday.
The $3.9 billion trust fund was created on July 1 to act as an investment conduit for workers compensation and state pension fund money.

The ruling by Kanawha County Circuit Court Judge Lynne Ranson said legislators violated the state's constitutional ban on equity investment of public funds when they created the fund. They had sought to evade the ban by making the trust fund an independent entity.
Craig Slaughter, executive director of the trust fund, said the ruling was expected and would be appealed.
"The next step is the (state) Supreme Court. We're pursuing that at all speed," Slaughter said. "It really hasn't changed my view of the whole thing at all to any significant extent."

The state Supreme Court blocked an earlier attempt by the state to put state pension money in the stock market. In that ruling, the justices suggested possible remedies, which the legislature used as a model when it established the independent trust fund in its last session, Slaughter said.
He described Ranson's ruling as a formality.
"Everybody's known all along it has to go to the Supreme Court," he said.

After the legislature approved the trust fund, state Attorney General Darrell McGraw and state treasury candidate Stan Klos sued to block the investments, alleging that they could only be authorized by constitutional amendment, which would require two-thirds voter approval.
Slaughter said he would pursue an amendment if the Supreme Court upheld Ranson's ruling. A ruling is expected as early as the Spring.

In the meantime, the trust fund will remain invested in U.S. Treasury bonds and high-grade corporate bonds. Slaughter has agreed not to invest any of the money in equities until the matter is settled.
Slaughter has argued that the investments would improve the pension fund's return and help divsersify the portfolio.

West Virginia had been one of only three states that did not allow the investment of public money in the stock market. The other two, South Carolina and Indiana, approved the investments in constitutional amendments approved by voters on Nov 5.
